## Objectives

- See what Module 2 adds to Module 1, and why it comes second
- Speak both dialects: the statistician's and the machine learner's
- State the unsupervised problem precisely — and see why it is harder to grade
- Check that R, RStudio and the course packages run on your machine

## [Section 1]{.section-kicker} Where we are {.section-slide background-color="#002f57"}

## Module 1 gave you a target

::: {.subtitle-frame}
Every method so far had a $y$
:::

- Regression: a number to predict — sales, length of stay, cost
- Logistic and Poisson: a class or a count
- Time series: tomorrow, from yesterday
- Ridge, LASSO: the same, with too many predictors

In every case the data came with **the answer attached**. The model's job was to reproduce it.

## Module 2 takes the target away — then gives it back

| Weeks | Question | Has a $y$? |
|---|---|---|
| 1–3 | *Which customers resemble each other?* — clustering, PCA, correspondence analysis | **No** |
| 4–6 | *Which will churn, default, be readmitted?* — trees, forests, boosting, neural networks | Yes |
| 7 | *Why did the model say that, and how do I tell the board?* | — |

::: {.callout-note}
The second half is supervised, like Module 1 — but with **algorithms** in place of **equations**. That change is the subject of this lecture.
:::

## [Section 2]{.section-kicker} Two dialects, one subject {.section-slide background-color="#002f57"}

## The same things, with different names

::: {.subtitle-frame}
Machine learning grew up next door to statistics and renamed the furniture
:::

| Statistics | Machine learning |
|---|---|
| Explanatory variable | **Input**, feature |
| Response variable | **Output**, target, label |
| Observations | **Training set** |
| Estimation, fitting | **Training** the model |
| Intercept | **Bias** |
| Transformation | **Activation function** |
| Coefficients, parameters | **Weights** |

You will hear both in this room. They are the same objects.

## What actually differs

- **Statistics** starts from a *sample* and reasons about a *population*. Standard errors, tests, confidence intervals — all of it lives there.
- **Machine learning** starts from a *training set* and is judged on a *test set*. There is no population in the picture. The question is only: does it predict well on data it has not seen?
- Statistics tends to *impose* the form of the relationship; machine learning tries to *learn* it, whatever it is.

::: {.callout-important title="The trade you are about to make"}
Flexibility and interpretability pull in opposite directions. The further you move toward complex models, the more you predict and the less you can explain, test, or defend. Module 2 is about spending that budget deliberately.
:::

## Prediction is not inference — a manager's version

::: {.subtitle-frame}
Same model, two different questions
:::

- **Inference**: *does a loyalty card increase spend, and by how much?* — you need a coefficient you can trust, with an interval around it
- **Prediction**: *which of these 40 000 customers will spend most next quarter?* — you need a ranking that holds up, and you do not care why

Module 1 was mostly the first question. Module 2 is mostly the second. Confusing them is the most common analytical mistake in business, and the most expensive.

## [Section 3]{.section-kicker} The unsupervised problem {.section-slide background-color="#002f57"}

## No label, no error, no "correct"

::: {.subtitle-frame}
The problem stated plainly
:::

You have $n$ rows and $p$ columns — customers and their behaviour, patients and their measurements — and **nothing to predict**.

You are asked: is there *structure*? Do these rows fall into groups? Can $p$ columns be summarised by fewer?

- In supervised learning, a wrong prediction is a visible number: $y - \hat y$
- In unsupervised learning there is no $y$. **No residual, no accuracy, no test set.**
- Two analysts can produce two different segmentations of the same customers, and neither is *wrong*

## Then how do you judge it?

- **Internal coherence**: are the groups tight and far apart? (numbers exist — we will use them — but they measure geometry, not truth)
- **Stability**: does the structure survive a different sample, a different seed, a different $k$?
- **Usefulness**: can marketing *act* on the segments? Do clinicians *recognise* the patient groups?

::: {.callout-note}
That last criterion is not a soft one. A segmentation nobody can act on is a wrong segmentation, however tight its clusters.
:::

## The three tools of the next three weeks

| Tool | Question it answers | Business example |
|---|---|---|
| **Clustering** (k-means, hierarchical) | Which rows are alike? | Customer segments; patient case-mix groups |
| **Principal components** | Which few directions carry most of the variation? | The two or three drivers behind twenty survey items |
| **Correspondence analysis** | How do two categorical variables relate? | Brands × attributes — the perception map |

All three are *descriptive*. They organise data; they do not predict anything. That is their strength and their limit.

## Every unsupervised method is a choice you make.  {.statement}

[What counts as "similar" is decided by you, not by the data.]{.muted}

## [Section 4]{.section-kicker} Setup check {.section-slide background-color="#002f57"}

## Ten minutes, now, on your own machine

Open RStudio, paste into the Console:

```{.r code-line-numbers="1|3-5|7"}
source("https://sbd-26-27.netlify.app/materials/setup.R")

library(tidyverse)
library(cluster)
library(factoextra)

fviz_nbclust(scale(USArrests), kmeans, method = "wss")
```

If a plot appears, you are ready for Tuesday. If not, that is what the next ten minutes and [office hours](../office-hours.html) are for — not Tuesday's lab.
